name: Marco Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me up here. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head shepherd on a hill farm, 1,100 ewes on about 2,000 hectares of rough grazing and moor. A normal day is the quad bike, two dogs and a lot of walking. I check the sheep on the high ground, fix fences the wind's had a go at, and in lambing season I basically live out there for six weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The space. Some mornings I'm above the cloud and the valley's just white below me. And I like the problem-solving. I've got a drone I use to find sheep in the gullies, and I ask an AI app about everything, from worm treatments to how to word a grant form. My boss thinks I'm a bit mad.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pay and isolation. Hill farming pays badly, and I put most of my savings into that drone, so I've got about two weeks' money in the bank. I'm single, I live in the farm cottage with my dog Pepper, and the nearest pub is eleven miles away. Winter can be lonely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's great, use it. I'd probably post a video of the drone finding a ewe stuck in a bog, which is my most popular thing ever, and say the AI helped me plan the flight. People like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I've already got. I use it every day and it makes me a bit faster. But it doesn't change what hill sheep are worth, which is not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep trying new uses. Maybe get it to sort the flock records so I can see which ewes keep losing lambs and sell them on. I'd ask my boss, Mr Lindqvist, to let me trial GPS collars on fifty ewes, if I could find a grant to pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the ewe in the bog.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March, a ewe heavy with lambs went missing in fog. I sent the drone up the gully with the heat camera and found her up to her shoulders in a bog. Got her out, she had twins the next day. Without the drone, I'd have found her dead in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your boss thinks you're mad. Does he ever come round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He did on the drone, after the bog. He said, 'Fine, but I'm not paying for the batteries.' So I pay for the batteries. That's partly why the savings are what they are.

S0.say: I'd say it's great and people should use it. I'd post a drone video and mention that AI helped me plan the flight.
S0.think: It's what I've already got: it makes me a bit faster. But it doesn't change what hill sheep are worth, which is not much.
S0.do: Uses AI to sort flock records and spot ewes that keep losing lambs. Asks his boss to trial GPS collars on fifty ewes, funded by a grant if he can find one.
S0.feel: Calm and a little excited by new tools.
S0.quote: He said, 'Fine, but I'm not paying for the batteries.' So I pay for the batteries.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is an enthusiast who puts his own thin savings into kit the farm won't pay for. The bog rescue is clearly a story he tells often and is proud of. His realism about sheep prices cuts through the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine. It gives people time to learn. I'd say the hill farms should get help to take up the good tools, because we're always last in line for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be ahead of most people round here, which is nice. But fewer beginners hired worries me for a different reason. Shepherds are getting older. If nobody takes on youngsters, in ten years it'll be me and a drone covering three farms, and I'll never get a day off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to show other farms in the valley how I use the drone and the AI, maybe for a small fee. I'd push for a young trainee to come up for lambing. And I'd apply for every grant there is for hill farm technology, because the paperwork is exactly what the AI's good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about being the last young shepherd in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd charge a small fee to show other farms. Would they pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Old Mr Davey down the valley rang me twice last winter to find sheep with the drone. I didn't charge him. Next time I might ask for diesel money, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old are the other shepherds in the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the youngest by about twenty years. The next youngest is Bryn, who's 49 and has a bad back. Most are in their sixties. When I go to the sheep sales, people call me 'the lad'.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is fine because people get time to learn. Hill farms should get help to take up the good tools, since we're always last in line.
S1.think: I'd be ahead of most people round here. But if nobody takes on young people, in ten years it'll be me and a drone covering three farms with no days off.
S1.do: Offers other valley farms help with drones and AI for a small fee or diesel money. Pushes for a young trainee at lambing and applies for hill farm technology grants, using AI for the forms.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some unease about being the last young shepherd in the valley.
S1.quote: When I go to the sheep sales, people call me 'the lad'.
S1.fieldNote: His slow-change worry is about a shrinking, ageing workforce rather than machines. He sees a small business in helping neighbours, though he hasn't charged anyone yet. He's open-handed and a bit lonely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough on office people, but there'll be new jobs, and some of those should be out here. I'd say the government should put the new money into rural broadband and training, not just cities. I'd say it online, because that's where I talk to people in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it barely touches me directly. But some of what I'd want to do, like selling lamb direct or doing drone work, needs customers with money. If office people are getting laid off, fewer of them pay extra for hill lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at those new AI-related jobs, out of curiosity, but most would be in cities. I'd try selling drone surveys for sheep and fences to other farms, maybe a hundred a day. And I'd keep my costs down, no new kit for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Curious too. Mixed, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the hills for one of those new jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it for about a day, then I'd look out of the window. No. Unless it paid triple, and even then, I'd miss the dogs too much. Pepper would hate a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no new kit for a year. How hard is that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very hard. There's a new thermal camera I've had my eye on for months. I'd sulk. But I've been down to a few days of money before, and I don't want to do that again.

S2.say: I'd say it's tough on office people but there'll be new jobs, and some should be in rural areas. The government should put money into rural broadband and training, not just cities.
S2.think: It barely touches me directly. But my ideas for selling lamb direct or drone work need customers with money, and laid-off office workers won't pay extra for hill lamb.
S2.do: Looks at the new AI jobs out of curiosity but stays put. Tries selling drone surveys of sheep and fences to other farms at about a hundred a day, and buys no new kit for a year.
S2.quote: I'd think about it for about a day, then I'd look out of the window.
S2.fieldNote: His centre view shows in wanting government help aimed at rural areas without taking sides. He's open to change but clearly tied to the hills and his dogs. Giving up new kit is a real sacrifice for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains need sharing fairly, but I'd be careful saying how. People round here vote all sorts, and I don't want to fall out with neighbours I need at lambing. I'd say, let's see real plans, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it could go two ways for me. City people with new money might buy hill land for fun or for nature schemes, and some of them might pay a skilled shepherd to manage it. Or they might plant trees on all of it and not need sheep at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd reach out to estate agents and land managers and say, here's what I can do: livestock, drones, habitat surveys. I'd learn about nature payments, the money the government gives for things like peat bog restoration. And I'd keep Mr Lindqvist close, because if he sells, I want to be part of the deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a bit of opportunity in it. I'd be lying awake planning, not worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the trees-instead-of-sheep worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's already happening in the next valley. A company bought a hill farm, planted it all with spruce for carbon credits, which is money from companies paying to make up for their pollution, and the shepherd there lost his job and his cottage. He's driving delivery vans now. That's the bit that keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lying awake planning, not worrying. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Some nights it's worrying dressed up as planning. With two weeks in the bank, any plan that goes wrong goes wrong fast.

S3.say: I'd say the gains need sharing fairly, but I'd want real plans, not slogans. I'd be careful, because I need my neighbours at lambing whatever way they vote.
S3.think: It could go two ways for me. Newly rich buyers might pay a skilled shepherd to manage hill land, or they might plant it all with trees and not need sheep at all.
S3.do: Contacts estate agents and land managers to offer livestock, drone and habitat survey skills. Learns about government nature payments such as peat bog restoration, and stays close to his boss in case the farm is sold.
S3.feel: Anxious but sensing opportunity, though some of his planning is worry in disguise.
S3.quote: Some nights it's worrying dressed up as planning.
S3.fieldNote: When I pushed on his upbeat answer, he admitted some of the planning is really worry. The neighbouring shepherd who lost his job to a tree plantation is a vivid, close-to-home warning. He positions himself as useful to whoever ends up owning the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms could be brilliant, and I'd mean it. A robot that walks the hill in a storm so I don't have to? Yes, please. But I'd also say we need rules so farm workers aren't just binned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the hill protects me a bit. Robots on flat dairy farms and in packing sheds, sure. On a 40-degree slope in sideways rain, with a ewe stuck under a rock? I'd want to see it. But in five years, they'll get better, and then I'm the expensive bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to be the person who runs the robots up here, not the person replaced by them. I'd ask the dealers if I could test one for free, as a hill trial. I'd learn the maintenance side, because out here, whoever can fix the machine is the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and excited at the same time. Scared for the older lads in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scared for the older lads. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bryn, mostly. He's 49 with a bad back, and a robot would do what his back can't. That sounds good until you realise it means they don't need Bryn. He's got two kids at the high school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it went wrong for you, with two weeks of savings, what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell the drone, which would break my heart. Then probably offer myself as a shepherd for hire around the valley, by the day. There's always someone needing help at lambing. It's not a living, but it buys time.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots could be brilliant, especially one that walks the hill in a storm for me. But we'd need rules so farm workers aren't just thrown away.
S4.think: The steep hill protects me a bit for now. But in five years the robots will improve, and then I'm the expensive part.
S4.do: Aims to be the one running robots on the hill, asking dealers for a free hill trial. Learns the maintenance side, and if things go wrong would sell the drone and work as a day shepherd around the valley.
S4.feel: Uneasy and excited at once, and scared for older shepherds in the valley.
S4.quote: On a 40-degree slope in sideways rain, with a ewe stuck under a rock? I'd want to see it.
S4.fieldNote: He's the least frightened of the robot scenario of anyone I'd expect, partly because of the terrain and partly his temperament. His fear goes to Bryn, the older shepherd with a bad back. Selling the drone is the measure of how bad things would have to get.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one without robots, oddly. The robots I can learn. But land being bought up and planted with trees, that's the one that could take my job and my home at once. What would help is rules that keep working farms working, and nature money that pays farmers to do the work, not just landowners.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about loneliness. Out here, the job is half your social life. If the job goes, it's not just money. You stop seeing anyone.

headlineQuote: Some nights it's worrying dressed up as planning.
portrait: Marco Schmidt is 27 and head shepherd for 1,100 ewes on a hill farm, living alone in the farm cottage with his dog Pepper, eleven miles from the nearest pub. He's an upbeat gadget lover who spent most of his savings on a drone and uses AI every day, and he keeps his politics careful because he needs his neighbours at lambing. He worries more about an ageing workforce and land being sold for tree planting than about robots, which he thinks he can learn to run. Under the enthusiasm, he admits some of his planning is worry in disguise, and he's quietly afraid for older shepherds like Bryn.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario without robots, because land being bought up and planted with trees could cost him both his job and his home.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that keep working farms working, and nature payments that pay farmers to do the work, not just landowners.
